lessons.title: Foundry projects, the model catalog, and deployments
lessons.summary: Learn how projects organize work, the catalog supports model choice, and deployments make models callable.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
Foundry solution work starts with the management boundary. A **Foundry resource** is the Azure resource that provides access to Foundry capabilities, identity, networking, policy, and endpoints. A **project** is the workspace inside that resource where developers organize app assets such as files, model deployments, evaluations, and agents. If you have seen older Azure AI Studio or hub-based terminology, treat it carefully: current Foundry investments emphasize Foundry resources and projects, while older hub/project experiences can still appear in some environments.

The **model catalog** is for discovery and comparison. A team can review model families, modalities, and supported scenarios before choosing a candidate. The catalog entry by itself is not what production code calls. To use a model from an app, the team creates a **deployment**. The deployment gives the model a configured name and endpoint routing target. In many SDK examples, the deployment name is passed as the model value so the request reaches the intended configured model.

Foundry playgrounds help teams test prompts, parameters, safety behavior, and sample inputs before writing code. The Code tab and SDK documentation then help developers move from prototype to a lightweight client. Authentication is another fundamentals decision: API keys can be used in some endpoint patterns, but Microsoft Entra ID with least-privilege Foundry roles is the preferred enterprise pattern because it avoids long-lived secrets and supports governance. A sound implementation checks that the deployment is ready, stores endpoint and deployment names in configuration, and includes monitoring or evaluation before broad use.

terminology.definition: A Foundry workspace for assets and development.
A place to discover and compare model capabilities.
A configured model target an app can call.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso support wants a chat helper for internal troubleshooting notes. The team creates a Foundry resource that meets its Azure policy requirements, then creates a project for the support prototype. In the catalog, the developers compare a fast low-cost model for short answers with a larger model for longer summaries. They deploy the selected model, test prompts in the playground with fictional support tickets, and only then connect a small web client.
lessons.technicalExample: A developer stores `PROJECT_ENDPOINT` and `DEPLOYMENT_NAME` as app settings. During startup, the client authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID using a managed identity or developer credential, creates a Foundry/OpenAI-compatible client for the project endpoint, and sends user prompts to the named deployment. Before release, the team runs a quick deployment-state check and uses playground results as seed examples for evaluation.

misconception.myth: Selecting a model in the catalog is enough for an application to use it.
misconception.reality: The catalog is a discovery surface. An app needs a deployed model or project endpoint target, plus authentication and configuration, before requests can be routed reliably.

lessons.examTakeaway: For AI-901, distinguish the resource/project that organizes work, the catalog that helps choose a model, the deployment that code calls, and the authentication method that controls access.
lessons.recap: A Foundry resource provides the Azure management boundary; a project organizes solution assets; the catalog helps compare models; and deployments make models callable. Playground testing reduces risk before code integration, while Microsoft Entra ID and least-privilege roles are preferable for governed applications.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of a Foundry project as a workshop. The model catalog is the tool shelf, a deployment is the tool installed at a workstation, and the endpoint plus authentication is the badge-controlled door your app uses to reach it.
lessons.anotherExample: Fabrikam tests two summarization models in the playground for call-center notes. It deploys the model that best follows the required format, stores the deployment name outside the code, and uses Entra-based access for the service that generates daily summaries.

lessons.title: Building agents: instructions, tools, and knowledge
lessons.summary: Learn how agent instructions, tools, knowledge, testing, and review fit a single-agent solution.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
A Foundry agent is more than a single model call. At fundamentals level, an agent combines a model with **instructions**, optional **tools**, optional **knowledge**, and a conversation state pattern. Instructions define the agent's job, boundaries, tone, escalation behavior, and safety rules. A good instruction set says what sources to trust, when to ask a clarifying question, and when the agent should not act.

Tools extend the agent beyond text generation. Common examples include knowledge or file search for retrieval, code interpreter for calculations or file analysis, and actions/functions that call an approved business API. A procurement agent might search policy files and draft a request, but require a manager approval tool before submission. A support agent might search a knowledge base, then create a ticket only when the answer is not found. The important design point is least capability: attach only the tools needed for the task.

Agents also need conversation handling. Foundry documentation uses current agent concepts such as conversations, items, responses, and agent versions; older Assistants-style terms such as threads can still appear in developer discussions or older material, so verify the current API names before publishing detailed steps. The principle is stable: the app must keep enough conversation context for multi-turn work while preventing data leakage between users. Testing should include normal tasks, missing knowledge, tool failures, and adversarial prompts. Responsible deployment adds tracing, evaluations, monitoring, and human review for high-impact actions.

terminology.definition: A model-based solution guided by instructions and optional tools.
Guidance for role, boundaries, and behavior.
A callable capability for retrieval or action.

lessons.businessScenario: Northwind Traders wants an internal inventory policy assistant. Employees ask whether a damaged item can be returned, whether a transfer needs approval, or how to open an exception. The team creates a prompt agent with a clear policy-support role, attaches approved inventory documents as knowledge, and adds one ticket-creation function for unresolved cases.
lessons.technicalExample: The agent instructions say: answer only from approved policy content, cite the relevant policy section when available, ask one clarifying question if the item type is missing, and create a ticket only after the user confirms. In testing, the team verifies that the agent searches files for policy questions, refuses payroll questions, and does not call the ticket tool for casual greetings.

misconception.myth: An agent becomes safer and smarter whenever you add more tools.
misconception.reality: Each tool expands what the agent can do and what can go wrong. Use narrow instructions, curated knowledge, tool descriptions, permissions, and review gates to control behavior.

lessons.examTakeaway: Recognize an agent as model plus instructions plus tools or knowledge. Choose a managed prompt agent for simple single-agent work and add governance before enabling actions.
lessons.recap: Instructions shape behavior, knowledge grounds answers, and tools let the agent retrieve information or take approved actions. Test the agent with realistic conversations and edge cases, then monitor tool use and output quality after release.
lessons.simplerExplanation: An agent is like a trained employee. The instructions are the job description, the knowledge source is the handbook, and tools are the approved systems the employee can use—but not every employee should have every system.
lessons.anotherExample: Woodgrove Bank creates an HR FAQ agent. It answers from benefits documents, escalates account-specific payroll questions, and uses a case-creation function only after the employee confirms the summary.

lessons.title: Text analysis and translation
lessons.summary: Use Azure Language for text analysis and Translator for multilingual content workflows.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
Text solutions usually ask one of two questions: *What does this text mean?* or *How should this text be expressed in another language?* Azure Language in Foundry Tools addresses the first question with natural language processing capabilities. Current core capabilities include language detection, personally identifiable information (PII) detection, named entity recognition (NER), custom NER, and text analytics for health. Existing or legacy scenarios can also include sentiment analysis, key phrase extraction, summarization, custom text classification, conversational language understanding, question answering, and orchestration workflows. For fundamentals content, focus on the scenario rather than memorizing every menu label.

NER extracts entities such as people, organizations, locations, dates, or domain-specific labels. PII detection identifies personal information that may need masking or special handling. Language detection helps route text to the correct processing or translation path. Sentiment and key phrases are useful for customer feedback analysis, while summarization condenses long text for review. Translation is a separate workload: Azure Translator converts text or documents across languages and can be used in multilingual applications.

A realistic solution often chains these capabilities. For example, a support app might detect the source language, identify PII, mask sensitive values for analytics, summarize the issue, and translate the approved summary for a regional team. Accuracy and responsible use matter because language models can miss nuance, domain terminology, sarcasm, or regulated content. For legal, medical, financial, or brand-sensitive text, include review and keep data retention minimal.

terminology.definition: Named entity recognition for people, places, and other entities.
Detection of personal information in text.
A Foundry Tool for language translation.

lessons.businessScenario: Woodgrove Bank receives support messages in multiple languages. The business wants to group issues by product, remove unnecessary personal information from analytics, translate selected summaries for a central operations team, and still preserve original messages for authorized case handlers.
lessons.technicalExample: The intake service first calls language detection. If the text is supported for downstream translation, it calls PII detection and masks phone numbers before analytics. It then uses entity recognition to find product names and branch locations, summarizes the issue for reporting, and uses Translator to produce an English operations summary. The original text is stored with tighter access controls.

misconception.myth: Translation and text analysis are the same capability because both process text.
misconception.reality: Translation changes language. Text analysis extracts meaning, labels, signals, or sensitive data from text. Many solutions use both, but they answer different questions.

lessons.examTakeaway: Choose Azure Language for analysis tasks such as entities, PII, sentiment, key phrases, language detection, and summarization. Choose Translator when the requirement is multilingual conversion.
lessons.recap: Text analysis finds meaning in text; translation rewrites content in another language. A responsible pipeline detects sensitive data, applies the right analysis or translation capability, and adds review for regulated or high-impact content.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Text analysis is like reading a message with a highlighter and labels. Translation is like rewriting the message for someone who speaks another language.
lessons.anotherExample: A retailer analyzes product reviews by detecting sentiment, extracting product names, summarizing common complaints, and translating selected reviews for regional product managers.

lessons.title: Speech to text and text to speech
lessons.summary: Use Speech to convert audio to text, text to audio, and spoken content between languages.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
Speech workloads add audio input, audio output, or multilingual spoken communication to an AI solution. **Speech to text** converts spoken audio into written text. It is used for dictation, captions, meeting transcripts, call-center analytics, and voice prompts that feed a model or agent. **Text to speech** converts written text into spoken audio using synthetic voices. It is used for accessibility, voice assistants, IVR systems, learning apps, and spoken responses from a generative solution.

**Speech translation** converts spoken language across languages, either to translated text or speech depending on the implementation. Speech solutions can also involve language identification, pronunciation assessment, batch transcription for stored audio, real-time transcription for live audio, and custom speech options for domain vocabulary. In Foundry scenarios, Azure Speech in Foundry Tools can be combined with a deployed multimodal model or agent: speech recognition turns the user's audio into text, the model or agent processes the request, and text to speech reads the answer back.

Quality depends on audio conditions and vocabulary. Background noise, multiple speakers, accents, microphones, and specialized product names can affect transcription. Custom vocabulary or custom speech models can improve domain-specific recognition. Responsible design includes informing users when voices are synthetic, protecting recordings and transcripts, avoiding unnecessary retention, and adding human review where spoken output might affect health, finance, safety, or legal decisions.

terminology.definition: Converts spoken language for multilingual scenarios.

lessons.businessScenario: Adventure Works builds a visitor kiosk for a museum exhibit. Visitors ask spoken questions about fictional artifacts. The kiosk transcribes the question, sends it to a Foundry agent grounded in approved exhibit notes, and reads the answer aloud in a friendly voice.
lessons.technicalExample: The client captures microphone audio and uses speech to text for real-time transcription. The transcript is sent to the agent with conversation context. The agent returns a concise answer and a confidence note. If the answer is safe to speak, text to speech synthesizes the response; otherwise the kiosk displays a message asking the visitor to contact staff.

misconception.myth: Speech to text and text to speech are interchangeable because both are speech services.
misconception.reality: They run in opposite directions. Speech to text understands audio input; text to speech produces audio output from text.

lessons.examTakeaway: Identify the direction of conversion: audio input needs speech to text, audio output needs text to speech, and multilingual spoken conversion points to speech translation.
lessons.recap: Speech solutions can transcribe, synthesize, translate, and identify spoken language. A voice-enabled Foundry app often combines speech to text, a model or agent, and text to speech, with privacy and review controls for recordings and output.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Speech to text is a note-taker listening to someone speak. Text to speech is a narrator reading written words aloud. Speech translation is an interpreter between languages.
lessons.anotherExample: A call center transcribes customer calls, summarizes action items, detects product names in the transcript, and sends a synthesized callback message only after an agent approves the wording.

lessons.title: Computer vision and image generation
lessons.summary: Separate visual understanding from creating new images, and add review for generated visuals.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
Vision and image generation are related but different. **Computer vision** interprets existing visual content. Azure Vision in Foundry Tools includes capabilities such as image analysis, OCR for printed or handwritten text, and face-related scenarios where appropriate policies allow them. Vision-enabled chat models add multimodal reasoning: a user can upload an image and ask questions about visible content, damage, layout, or context. If the goal is to understand an existing photo, diagram, screenshot, or receipt image, choose a vision or extraction capability.

**Image generation** creates new visual output from text prompts and, for some models, optional image inputs. It can support concept art, product mockups, storyboards, and marketing drafts. Prompt quality matters: specify subject, style, constraints, intended use, and what to avoid. Generated images should be treated as drafts until reviewed for accuracy, safety, accessibility, brand fit, and intellectual-property concerns.

Content safety is important in both directions. Visual input might contain personal data, people, unsafe scenes, or copyrighted material. Generated output might be misleading, unsafe, or inappropriate for the audience. A fundamentals-level design keeps generated images out of automatic publication, adds review, and avoids claiming that generated visuals are factual evidence. For OCR-heavy or structured document scenarios, Azure Document Intelligence or Content Understanding might be a better fit than a general vision chat prompt.

terminology.definition: A model that can reason over image input.

lessons.businessScenario: Alpine Ski House receives customer photos of damaged rental equipment and also needs draft banner images for a winter campaign. The operations team wants visual inspection notes from uploaded photos, while marketing wants creative drafts that a human designer can approve or revise.
lessons.technicalExample: The claims app sends uploaded equipment photos to a vision-enabled model with instructions to describe visible damage, avoid identifying people, and flag unclear images for review. Separately, the marketing workflow sends approved text prompts to an image-generation model, stores generated drafts in a review queue, and records the prompt used for traceability.

misconception.myth: Any image-related requirement should use image generation.
misconception.reality: Image generation creates new visuals. Use vision, OCR, Document Intelligence, or Content Understanding when the requirement is to inspect, read, or extract information from existing visuals.

lessons.examTakeaway: Separate visual understanding from visual creation. Choose vision-enabled models or OCR for existing images, and image generation for new visual drafts with safety review.
lessons.recap: Vision interprets images; OCR reads text in images; image generation creates new images. Responsible implementations review generated output, protect sensitive visual data, and choose structured extraction tools when exact fields are needed.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Vision is looking at a picture and explaining what is there. Image generation is drawing a new picture from instructions. OCR is reading words inside the picture.
lessons.anotherExample: A retailer uses a vision-enabled model to describe shelf photos for planogram checks, OCR to read shelf labels, and image generation to draft seasonal display concepts for a designer to approve.

lessons.title: Extracting information from documents and content
lessons.summary: Use Content Understanding to extract structured fields from documents, images, audio, and video.
learningObjectives: Identify the Foundry capability for the scenario
lessons.explanation:
Information extraction turns unstructured content into structured data that software can route, validate, search, or analyze. In Foundry Tools, **Azure Content Understanding** is positioned for multimodal extraction from documents, images, audio, and video into user-defined outputs. It can help create schema-aligned fields, classifications, summaries, evidence, and confidence signals from messy real-world content. **Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools** remains important for intelligent document processing, OCR, layout, prebuilt document models such as invoices or receipts, and custom document models. Microsoft Learn notes that Document Intelligence provides deterministic extraction for structured documents, while Content Understanding adds LLM-powered analyzers for complex, unstructured, and multimodal content.

A good extraction design begins with the output contract. Decide which fields are required, what data type each field should have, and what evidence or confidence is needed. For invoices, the fields might include vendor, invoice number, date, subtotal, tax, and total. For call recordings, they might include customer intent, sentiment, promised action, and callback date. For videos, they might include topics, speakers, scenes, or compliance flags.

Human review is part of the architecture, not a failure. Low-confidence values, missing evidence, high-value transactions, regulated fields, and contradictory documents should route to a reviewer. A lightweight app can call the analyzer, store extracted fields with confidence and source evidence, and send exceptions to a queue. Because Content Understanding and Document Intelligence naming, API versions, and preview capabilities can change, keep needsVerification enabled for portal- or version-specific details.

terminology.definition: A Foundry Tool for multimodal extraction.
A schema or configuration for extracting fields.
A signal that can trigger human review.

lessons.businessScenario: Litware processes supplier invoices, delivery-label photos, support-call recordings, and training videos. Staff need structured fields for automation but also evidence and confidence so they can review uncertain values before payments, customer follow-up, or compliance reporting.
lessons.technicalExample: The intake workflow classifies each file. Structured invoices use a Document Intelligence prebuilt or custom model to extract fields and layout. Mixed media and complex packets use Content Understanding analyzers that output a schema with field values, confidence, and grounding evidence. Values below the review threshold or above a business-risk threshold are sent to a human queue.

misconception.reality: A summary is narrative text. Extraction produces structured fields, classifications, and evidence that downstream systems can validate and act on.

lessons.examTakeaway: Choose Content Understanding for multimodal structured extraction, and recognize Document Intelligence for document OCR, layout, prebuilt models, and custom document processing.
lessons.recap: Extraction solutions define fields, process content, return values with evidence or confidence, and route exceptions for review. Documents, images, audio, and video may require different analyzers or tools depending on structure and risk.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Information extraction is like turning a messy pile of papers, photos, calls, and videos into a checked spreadsheet, with sticky notes showing where each value came from.
lessons.anotherExample: A mortgage team extracts borrower names and property addresses from forms with Document Intelligence, then uses Content Understanding to analyze supporting photos and call recordings for missing-document evidence.
